newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Euro cen. banks not copying German gold plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Euro cen. banks not copying German gold plan.

text.p: Most European central banks have no plans to copy Germany's suprise plan to revalue its near-3,000 tonne gold reserves to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU), spokesmen said on Friday.
Several have no need to anyway, since they already price their stocks much closer to current market prices than the ultra-conservative Bundesbank has to date, they explained.
On the international gold market, bullion was fixed in London at $344.50 on Friday afternoon, sharply lower than the morning fixing of $347.00.
Analysts said revaluing gold reserves undermined Bonn's credibility and might not help it to meet the Maastricht budget deficit target of 3.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

"It all smacks of a German government hitting the panic button," said David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns in London. "What they are actually doing is opening up the whole EMU game to creative accounting methods."

Graham McDevitt, economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London said: "The fact that a lot more fudges are being used, rather than structural adjustments, does lend itself to the view that we could have a weaker euro."

The plan was a frantic stop-gap measure after an official tax estimate showed that Finance Minister Theo Waigel would have 18 billion marks ($10.6 billion) less revenue this year than planned. But it appeared to conform to the letter of European Union guidelines on valuing a country's gold and currency reserves.

However, it clearly violated the spirit of Germany's hardline stand on the single currency and provoked hoots of criticism from Italy -- the target of several stern German lectures on clean accounting in the past -- and even at home.
The central banks of Austria, Britain, Denmark, Finland, Ireland, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden all told Reuters they had no plans to boost their bullion's book value.

Their counterparts in France, Italy and Belgium had no comment. The European Commission was not sure whether Eurostat, its statistical watchdog, had to approve the plan. "We are waiting to see what the details are," an EU spokesman said. "There will be no fudging of the figures."
Few details of the plan were available and government sources said some Bundesbank council members doubted they could revalue the reserves and top up Bonn's coffers this year.
But a finance ministry spokeswoman said the bank, which usually draws up its accounts at the year end, could produce an interim account with the higher values.
There was some harsh criticism for Waigel's plan, which German newspapers lambasted as "witchcraft" and Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini warned could jeopardise the whole EMU.

"I would be very surprised if the German government were to have recourse to accounting gimmicks such as the use of asset sales or a revaluation in order to meet a revenue shortfall for 1997," Dini told the International Herald Tribune.

"This would open up a wider gap than expected in 1998, thus making precarious the respect and sustainability of the stability pact. By doing this, Germany could put in jeopardy the healthy functioning of European monetary union," he warned.

A Reuters survey showed European central banks valued their gold in different ways. Few were as prudent as the Bundesbank, which books its assets at their all-time lowest price or at the purchase price according to German book-keeping regulations.

The Bank of France revalues its gold every six months to reflect market prices while the Belgian and Danish central banks did the same annually. Italy's gold is also near market value, in line with a formula approved by the European Monetary Institute (EMI), the forerunner of Europe's central bank.
The Dutch Central Bank adjusts the value of its reserves every three years, basing the new total on the lowest average market price for the period minus 30 percent.
A Bank of Portugal spokesman said: "It makes no sense to revalue our reserves as the accounting value is close to the market value."

The Belgian central bank has pioneered the sale of gold stocks, reducing its bullion from 1,300 tonnes in 1990 to 600 tonnes now. Its last sale was in March 1996, when it sold 203 tonnes to an unspecified central bank.
A German currency expert slammed the plan as "cooking the books" and warned that the move could be unconstitutional.

Wilhelm Hankel, a former German economics and finance ministry adviser, told the Berliner Zeitung daily that if a listed company were to behave in the same way it would lose all credibility with the banks and its shareholders.

Frankfurt analysts said the revaluation plan should be largely neutral for money supply growth, keeping inflationary pressures in check. While they did not know how large the future transfers might be, they agreed the Bundesbank had plenty of tools to drain excess liqudity.
